newsitem.title: COSTA RICA: FOCUS - Coffee trade ponders ACPC caution.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Coffee trade ponders ACPC caution.

text.p: Coffee traders and analysts pondered Sunday why the world's most powerful producers' group opted to take a defensive forward-looking stance just when market prices appear to be at the mercy of their export limit plan.
"They have the market by the jugular and instead of taking decisive steps, they are cautious, they are on a peculiar defensive," said one U.S. trader who declined to be named.

Member nations of the Association of Coffee Producing Countries' (ACPC) technical group were expected to suggest modifications to the coffee cartel's export programme to at least keep the squeeze on coffee supplies, one of the major reasons for upward trending prices.

But the ACPC group, here in this tiny Central American capital for a lightning one-day meeting, made no announcements on tweaking the export plans. Instead, the ACPC issued a press release that made no reference to export volumes and highlighted the chairman's power to call extraordinary meetings if the situation merited such action.

"There is no mention of export volumes, instead they make a vague attempt to hint that consumption is higher than production, and they also refuse to give stock levels of producer countries," said a coffee analyst, who also asked to remain anonymous, reading into the short 10-paragraph statement.

ACPC nations have in place a coffee export programme to limit green coffee exports to 53.3 million 60-kg bags between July 1996 and June 1997 compared to its programme a cycle earlier of 45.8 million bags. The basic aim is to limit supply so that prices rise.

The cartel groups the globe's biggest producer nations and the 14-member council accounts for more than 80 percent of world production, although a handful of medium-sized rogue producer nations, such as Mexico and Guatemala, are not members.

Roberio Oliveira, the ACPC secretary-general, told reporters after the closed-door meeting that the 1996-1997 export programme was on line and he dismissed notions that ACPC nations were exporting beyond agreed limits.
"From the figures we have we could see the programme, the target will be achieved," Oliveira said refering to internal evaluations of the export limit plan.

Oliveira and ACPC Chairman Rubens Barbosa said proposals for modifications to the export programme, which were widely expected to be the hot topic at the meeting, did not come up in discussions. The statement made no reference to any such proposals, either.
The reiterance of the chairman's power to call extraordinary meetings was also seen as a defensive move and as a signal to markets that this could happen, sources said.

"The technical group will meet regularly at the end of the quarter to assess the implementation of the programme. If the situation so merits, the chairman of the ACPC shall convene a council meeting which will decide on the measures to be applied," the statement said.
Still, the first real signs of prices rising because of a shortage of coffee flows are being seen. Many point directly to the ACPC export limits and its squeezing supplies as the main reason.

Last week, December contracts in New York surged to fresh 11-week highs, largely on news that certified U.S. stocks fell to only 804 60-kg bags in the week, the equivalent of just three trading lots of coffee on the market.

Information about industry purchases and roasting levels in the United States suggests that coffee being bought by trade is being roasted immediately, sources said, another indicator of the supply squeeze.

"Traders and roasters have openly admitted to me that they have started to hate the ACPC, which means that something is working (with the plan)," said one Central American delegate at the San Jose gathering which was attended by delegates from Brazil, Colombia, Ivory Coast, El Salvador, Indonesia and Uganda and also by Costa Rica, Honduras as observers.

Such overt opposition to the cartel and its grip on the market make it even more puzzling why the ACPC technical group erred on the side of caution when member nations are calling for more strident action to boost prices.

Costa Rica coffee czar Alonso Lara, the chairman of the National Coffee Institute, said in letter to the ACPC that the cartel should be thinking about implementing automatic adjustment mechanisms on export limits when prices dip below $125 per 100 pounds.

Lara, out of the country on business, said the ACPC should also evaluate establishing differentials above market prices and the use of closing coffee export registers to boost prices. Also he suggested "abandoning international markets as the only parameter for fixing world coffee prices."
